questions.q: Who was president of the United States during the Civil War?
questions.explain: Abraham Lincoln took office in March 1861, just as Southern states were seceding, and led the Union until his death in April 1865.

questions.q: Who served as president of the Confederate States of America during the Civil War?
questions.explain: Jefferson Davis, a former U.S. senator from Mississippi, led the Confederacy from 1861 until its collapse in 1865.

questions.q: Which general commanded the Confederacy's Army of Northern Virginia?
questions.explain: Robert E. Lee led the Army of Northern Virginia from 1862 until he surrendered it at Appomattox in April 1865.

questions.q: Arlington National Cemetery was created during the Civil War on the estate of which Confederate general's family?
questions.explain: The Union Army took over the Lee family's Arlington estate early in the war and began burying soldiers there in 1864.

questions.q: Where did Robert E. Lee surrender to Ulysses S. Grant in April 1865?
questions.explain: Lee surrendered at Appomattox Court House on April 9, 1865, which effectively ended the Civil War.

questions.q: At which fort in Charleston Harbor were the first shots of the Civil War fired in April 1861?
questions.explain: Confederate guns fired on the Union garrison at Fort Sumter on April 12, 1861, and the fort surrendered the next day.

questions.q: In which year did the Civil War begin?
questions.explain: Fighting began at Fort Sumter in April 1861, a few weeks after Abraham Lincoln took office.

questions.q: In which year did the Civil War end?
questions.explain: Lee surrendered in April 1865 and the last Confederate forces gave up in the weeks that followed.

questions.q: Where was Abraham Lincoln shot on April 14, 1865?
questions.explain: Lincoln was shot while watching the play Our American Cousin at Ford's Theatre in Washington and died the next morning.

questions.q: What was John Wilkes Booth's profession?
questions.explain: Booth was a well-known actor from a famous theater family, which let him move freely around Ford's Theatre.

questions.q: Which 1863 speech by Abraham Lincoln begins 'Four score and seven years ago'?
questions.explain: Lincoln gave the Gettysburg Address on November 19, 1863. Its words are carved on the south wall of the Lincoln Memorial.

questions.q: Lincoln gave the Gettysburg Address at the dedication of what?
questions.explain: The speech dedicated the Soldiers' National Cemetery at Gettysburg, where Union dead from the July 1863 battle were buried.

questions.q: Lincoln's Gettysburg Address is famous partly for being short. About how long did it take him to deliver?
questions.explain: The address is under 300 words. Edward Everett, the main speaker that day, talked for about two hours.

questions.q: What did the Emancipation Proclamation do?
options: Declared enslaved people in Confederate areas free
Gave Black men the right to vote
questions.explain: The 1863 proclamation freed enslaved people in areas still in rebellion. The 13th Amendment ended slavery everywhere in 1865.

questions.q: Which amendment to the Constitution abolished slavery in the United States?
questions.explain: Congress passed the 13th Amendment in January 1865 and it was ratified that December, ending slavery nationwide.

questions.q: Which amendment made everyone born in the United States a citizen and promised 'equal protection of the laws'?
questions.explain: Ratified in 1868, the 14th Amendment granted citizenship to formerly enslaved people and is the basis of many civil rights cases.

questions.q: Which amendment, ratified in 1870, barred denying the vote because of race?
questions.explain: The 15th Amendment protected Black men's right to vote, though Southern states later used poll taxes and literacy tests to get around it.

questions.q: Which July 1863 battle in Pennsylvania is often called the turning point of the Civil War?
questions.explain: The Union victory at Gettysburg ended Lee's invasion of the North. It was the deadliest battle of the war.

questions.q: Which Union general led the 1864 'March to the Sea' from Atlanta to Savannah?
questions.explain: Sherman's army destroyed railroads, crops and supplies across Georgia to break the South's ability to keep fighting.

questions.q: What was the Underground Railroad?
options: An early subway line in New York
A secret network that helped people escape slavery
A canal linking the Great Lakes
questions.explain: The Underground Railroad was a network of routes and safe houses that helped enslaved people reach free states and Canada.

questions.q: Which woman escaped slavery and then returned to the South many times to guide others to freedom?
questions.explain: Harriet Tubman led dozens of people out of slavery in Maryland and later served the Union Army as a scout and spy.

questions.q: Which famous abolitionist, who escaped slavery and became a great speaker and writer, lived at Cedar Hill in Washington, D.C.?
questions.explain: Frederick Douglass bought the Cedar Hill house in Anacostia in 1877 and lived there until his death in 1895.

questions.q: Who wrote Uncle Tom's Cabin, the 1852 novel that turned many Northerners against slavery?
questions.explain: Uncle Tom's Cabin became the best-selling novel of the 1800s and stirred antislavery feeling across the North.

questions.q: Which political party did Abraham Lincoln belong to when he was elected president?
questions.explain: Lincoln, a former Whig, won the 1860 election as the candidate of the new Republican Party, founded in 1854 to oppose slavery's spread.

questions.q: Which state did Abraham Lincoln call home when he was elected president?
questions.explain: Lincoln was born in Kentucky and grew up in Indiana, but he built his law and political career in Springfield, Illinois.

questions.q: Which nickname did Abraham Lincoln earn for his reputation for fairness?
questions.explain: Lincoln was called Honest Abe from his days as a store clerk and lawyer in Illinois.

questions.q: During the Civil War, what name was commonly used for the Northern side?
questions.explain: The Northern states were called the Union; the 11 seceded Southern states formed the Confederacy.

questions.q: Which city was the capital of the Confederacy for most of the Civil War?
questions.explain: The Confederate capital moved from Montgomery, Alabama, to Richmond in 1861. Union troops took Richmond in April 1865.

questions.q: Which state was the first to secede from the Union, in December 1860?
questions.explain: South Carolina seceded on December 20, 1860, weeks after Lincoln's election. Ten more states followed.

questions.q: Which issue was at the heart of the conflict between North and South that led to the Civil War?
options: Slavery and its spread to the West
questions.explain: Secession followed Lincoln's election on a platform of keeping slavery out of the western territories.

questions.q: The 54th Massachusetts Infantry, shown in the movie Glory, was one of the first Union regiments made up of which soldiers?
questions.explain: The 54th Massachusetts became famous for its 1863 assault on Fort Wagner, South Carolina. About 180,000 Black men served in the Union Army.

questions.q: How is Abraham Lincoln shown in the giant statue inside the Lincoln Memorial?
questions.explain: Daniel Chester French's marble statue shows Lincoln seated. The memorial was dedicated in 1922.

questions.q: Whose portrait appears on both the U.S. penny and the five-dollar bill?
questions.explain: Lincoln's portrait has been on the penny since 1909, the 100th anniversary of his birth, and on the $5 bill since 1914.

questions.q: Which Civil War nurse founded the American Red Cross in 1881?
questions.explain: Clara Barton, called the 'Angel of the Battlefield,' cared for wounded soldiers and later founded the American Red Cross.

questions.q: Who became president after Abraham Lincoln was assassinated?
questions.explain: Vice President Andrew Johnson of Tennessee was sworn in on April 15, 1865, the morning Lincoln died.

questions.q: Which president became the first to be impeached by the House, in 1868?
questions.explain: The House impeached Andrew Johnson in 1868; the Senate fell one vote short of removing him from office.

questions.q: What is the period after the Civil War, when the South was brought back into the Union and freedpeople sought equal rights, called?
questions.explain: Reconstruction lasted from 1865 to 1877. It brought three amendments and the first Black members of Congress.

questions.q: Which group formed in the South after the Civil War and used violence to terrorize Black Americans and their allies?
questions.explain: The Klan was founded in Tennessee in 1865 or 1866. Congress passed the Enforcement Acts of 1870-1871 to fight it.

questions.q: Thousands of 'forty-niners' rushed to which place after gold was discovered there in 1848?
questions.explain: Gold found at Sutter's Mill in January 1848 set off the California Gold Rush, and California became a state in 1850.

questions.q: What was driven at Promontory Summit, Utah, in 1869 to mark the completion of the first transcontinental railroad?
questions.explain: On May 10, 1869, a ceremonial golden spike joined the Union Pacific and Central Pacific railroads.

questions.q: What did the United States gain from Mexico at the end of the Mexican-American War in 1848?
options: California and much of the Southwest
questions.explain: In the Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo, Mexico gave up California and land that became Nevada, Utah and parts of other states.

questions.q: The United States bought Alaska in 1867 from which country, a deal critics called 'Seward's Folly'?
questions.explain: Secretary of State William Seward arranged the $7.2 million purchase. Alaska later proved rich in gold, fish and oil.

questions.q: In the 1857 Dred Scott decision, what did the Supreme Court rule about Black Americans?
options: They could vote in every state
They had to be freed at age 21
They could not be U.S. citizens
questions.explain: The Dred Scott ruling also said Congress could not ban slavery in the territories, deepening the split between North and South.

questions.q: Abolitionist John Brown led an 1859 raid on a federal arsenal in which Virginia town?
questions.explain: John Brown hoped to start a slave uprising. He was captured, tried and hanged, and many Northerners saw him as a martyr.

questions.q: Which Confederate general earned the nickname 'Stonewall' at the First Battle of Bull Run?
questions.explain: Another general pointed to Jackson's brigade standing 'like a stone wall.' Jackson was killed by friendly fire in 1863.

questions.q: What kind of hat is Abraham Lincoln famous for wearing?
questions.explain: Lincoln's tall stovepipe hat made him look even taller than his 6 feet 4 inches. One he wore is at the Smithsonian.

questions.q: In 1858, Lincoln held a famous series of debates with which Illinois senator?
questions.explain: Lincoln lost the 1858 Senate race to Stephen Douglas, but the debates made him nationally known.

questions.q: The first major battle of the Civil War, in July 1861 near Manassas, Virginia, is known by which name?
questions.explain: The Confederate win at the First Battle of Bull Run showed both sides the war would be long and costly.

questions.q: Which 1862 Maryland battle is known as the bloodiest single day in American history?
questions.explain: About 23,000 men were killed, wounded or missing at Antietam on September 17, 1862. Lincoln then issued the preliminary Emancipation Proclamation.

questions.q: Juneteenth, now a federal holiday, marks the day in 1865 when news of freedom reached enslaved people in which state?
questions.explain: On June 19, 1865, Union general Gordon Granger announced in Galveston that all enslaved people in Texas were free.

questions.q: Which formerly enslaved woman gave the famous 1851 speech known as 'Ain't I a Woman?'
questions.explain: Sojourner Truth spoke at a women's rights convention in Akron, Ohio, linking the fight against slavery with women's rights.

questions.q: In the Civil War, Union soldiers usually wore blue uniforms. What color did Confederate soldiers usually wear?
questions.explain: Confederate uniforms were usually gray or a brownish 'butternut,' which is why the war is called a fight of the blue and the gray.

questions.q: Abraham Lincoln was famously born in what kind of home?
questions.explain: Lincoln was born on February 12, 1809, in a one-room log cabin in Kentucky.

questions.q: Which state was formed during the Civil War when its western counties broke away from Virginia?
questions.explain: Western Virginians opposed secession, and West Virginia joined the Union as a separate state in 1863.

questions.q: Washington, D.C., lay between Virginia and which slave state that stayed in the Union?
questions.explain: Keeping Maryland in the Union was vital, since losing it would have surrounded the capital with Confederate territory.

questions.q: Which Civil War song did Julia Ward Howe write in 1861?
questions.explain: Howe wrote new words to the tune of 'John Brown's Body.' The song became a Union anthem.

questions.q: Which poet mourned Abraham Lincoln in the poem 'O Captain! My Captain!'?
questions.explain: Walt Whitman, who had worked in Washington's Civil War hospitals, wrote the poem after Lincoln's assassination in 1865.

questions.q: Which president is often called the 'Great Emancipator'?
questions.explain: Lincoln earned the title by issuing the Emancipation Proclamation and pushing the 13th Amendment through Congress.

questions.q: Which Civil War general later served two terms as the 18th president?
questions.explain: Grant was elected president in 1868 and again in 1872. McClellan and Hancock both ran for president and lost.

questions.q: Ulysses S. Grant's portrait appears on which U.S. bill?
questions.explain: Grant has been on the $50 bill since 1913. Hamilton is on the $10, Jackson on the $20 and Franklin on the $100.

questions.q: Paper money first printed by the federal government during the Civil War got which nickname?
questions.explain: The Legal Tender Act of 1862 created national paper notes printed with green ink on the back, so people called them greenbacks.

questions.q: The Secret Service was created in 1865 to do what?
questions.explain: Fake bills were a huge problem after the war. The Secret Service did not formally protect presidents until after 1901.

questions.q: In December 1863, during the Civil War, the Statue of Freedom was placed on top of what?
questions.explain: Work on the Capitol's cast-iron dome went on through the war, and the bronze Statue of Freedom was raised to its top in 1863.

questions.q: Why is the Washington Monument two slightly different colors?
options: Building stopped for years, then new stone was used
One side faces the sun more often
It was damaged by fire in the Civil War
It was painted two colors on purpose
questions.explain: Work stopped in 1854 for lack of money and the Civil War, and resumed in 1879 with stone from a different quarry.

questions.q: When it was finished in 1884, what record did the Washington Monument hold?
questions.explain: At about 555 feet the monument was the world's tallest structure until the Eiffel Tower opened in 1889.

questions.q: After the Civil War, which promise referred to giving land to freed people?
questions.explain: General Sherman's 1865 order set aside land for freed families, but President Johnson soon gave most of it back to former owners.

questions.q: After the Civil War, many freed people farmed land owned by others in exchange for part of the crop. What was this system called?
questions.explain: Sharecroppers often fell deep into debt to landowners and stores, which kept many families poor for generations.

questions.q: Laws passed by Southern states right after the Civil War to limit the rights of freed people were called what?
questions.explain: The Black Codes of 1865-1866 restricted work, travel and property. Congress answered with the Civil Rights Act of 1866 and the 14th Amendment.

questions.q: Howard University in Washington, D.C., founded in 1867, is one of the best-known what?
questions.explain: Howard was named for General Oliver O. Howard, head of the Freedmen's Bureau. Frederick Douglass served on its board.

questions.q: In 1870, Hiram Revels of Mississippi became the first Black member of which body?
questions.explain: Revels took a Senate seat once held by Jefferson Davis. Joseph Rainey became the first Black House member later in 1870.

questions.q: Which inventor, known as the 'Wizard of Menlo Park,' developed a practical electric light bulb in 1879?
questions.explain: Edison's lab in Menlo Park, New Jersey, produced a long-lasting bulb in 1879 and later full electric power systems.

questions.q: Which machine for recording and playing back sound did Thomas Edison invent in 1877?
questions.explain: Edison's first phonograph recorded sound on tinfoil. He tested it by reciting 'Mary Had a Little Lamb.'

questions.q: Who received the patent for the telephone in 1876?
questions.explain: Bell's first words over the telephone were to his assistant: 'Mr. Watson, come here, I want to see you.'

questions.q: Where did the Wright brothers make the first powered airplane flights in December 1903?
questions.explain: They flew near Kitty Hawk on December 17, 1903, because the area had steady winds and soft sand for landings.

questions.q: Which two brothers built the 1903 Flyer, the first successful powered airplane, now displayed at the National Air and Space Museum?
questions.explain: Orville piloted the first 12-second flight on December 17, 1903. The Flyer has been at the Smithsonian since 1948.

questions.q: Before building airplanes, what kind of business did Wilbur and Orville Wright run in Dayton, Ohio?
questions.explain: Their bicycle shop paid for their flight experiments, and their mechanics helped build the engine for the Flyer.

questions.q: Which car did Henry Ford introduce in 1908 that made automobiles affordable for millions of Americans?
questions.explain: Ford sold about 15 million Model Ts between 1908 and 1927, and its price fell as his factories got faster.

questions.q: Which Gilded Age businessman made a fortune in steel and later paid to build thousands of public libraries?
questions.explain: Andrew Carnegie sold his steel company in 1901 and gave away most of his wealth, funding more than 2,500 libraries.

questions.q: John D. Rockefeller became one of the richest Americans through which company?
questions.explain: At its peak around 1880 Standard Oil controlled about 90 percent of U.S. oil refining. The Supreme Court broke it up in 1911.

questions.q: Cornelius Vanderbilt built his fortune mainly in which businesses?
questions.explain: The 'Commodore' made money in steamboats first, then took control of the New York Central Railroad.

questions.q: Which author helped give the 'Gilded Age' its name through an 1873 novel he co-wrote?
questions.explain: Mark Twain and Charles Dudley Warner wrote The Gilded Age, mocking an era that looked golden but hid greed and corruption.

questions.q: Who wrote the novels The Adventures of Tom Sawyer and Adventures of Huckleberry Finn?
questions.explain: Samuel Clemens wrote as Mark Twain. Huckleberry Finn, published in 1884-1885, is often called the great American novel.

questions.q: Which inventor, working with George Westinghouse, championed alternating current (AC) electricity?
questions.explain: Tesla's AC system won out over Edison's direct current and powers most homes today.

questions.q: Which invention did Samuel Morse demonstrate in 1844 with a message sent from the U.S. Capitol to Baltimore?
questions.explain: Morse's first official message, 'What hath God wrought,' was sent from the Capitol on May 24, 1844.

questions.q: Who was the first president to serve two terms that were not back to back?
questions.explain: Grover Cleveland won in 1884, lost to Benjamin Harrison in 1888 and won again in 1892.

questions.q: Which park, created by Congress in 1872, was the world's first national park?
questions.explain: President Grant signed the law creating Yellowstone, which spreads across parts of Wyoming, Montana and Idaho.

questions.q: Which waterway, opened by the United States in 1914, connected the Atlantic and Pacific oceans?
questions.explain: The Panama Canal saved ships a long trip around South America. The U.S. handed it over to Panama in 1999.

questions.q: Which country gave the Statue of Liberty to the United States, dedicated in 1886?
questions.explain: The statue was a gift from the people of France to honor American independence and the friendship of the two nations.

questions.q: Ellis Island, which opened in 1892, was the main entry station for immigrants arriving in which city?
questions.explain: More than 12 million immigrants passed through Ellis Island in New York Harbor before it closed in 1954.

questions.q: The immigration station on Angel Island, which processed many arrivals from Asia, was in which bay?
questions.explain: Angel Island station opened in 1910. Many Chinese immigrants were held there for weeks or months under the exclusion laws.

questions.q: Which 1882 law was the first major U.S. law to bar immigrants of a specific nationality?
questions.explain: The Chinese Exclusion Act banned Chinese laborers for ten years. It was renewed and not repealed until 1943.

questions.q: Many immigrants in cities like New York around 1900 lived in crowded apartment buildings called what?
questions.explain: Tenements were often dark and poorly ventilated, and whole families might share one or two rooms.

questions.q: Labor Day, made a federal holiday in 1894, honors whom?
questions.explain: Congress made the first Monday in September a national holiday for workers in 1894, after years of labor parades.

questions.q: Around 1900, most new immigrants to the United States came from which region?
questions.explain: Millions of Italians, Poles, Jews from the Russian Empire, Greeks and others arrived between 1890 and 1914.

questions.q: In the late 1840s, a famine caused by a potato blight drove huge numbers of people from which country to the United States?
questions.explain: The Great Famine killed about a million people in Ireland, and well over a million more emigrated, many to American cities.

questions.q: Thousands of workers from which country did much of the hardest work building the Central Pacific Railroad through the Sierra Nevada?
questions.explain: Chinese workers made up most of the Central Pacific's labor force, blasting tunnels through the mountains in brutal conditions.

questions.q: At which 1876 battle were George Custer and his troops defeated by Lakota and Cheyenne warriors?
questions.explain: Custer and more than 200 soldiers were killed at the Little Bighorn in Montana Territory in June 1876.

questions.q: Which Lakota leader is famous for uniting his people against U.S. forces at the Battle of the Little Bighorn?
questions.explain: Sitting Bull, a Hunkpapa Lakota holy man, later toured with Buffalo Bill's Wild West and was killed in 1890.

questions.q: Geronimo was a famous leader of which Native American people?
questions.explain: Geronimo resisted U.S. and Mexican forces in the Southwest until he surrendered in 1886.

questions.q: The 1890 massacre of Lakota people by U.S. soldiers in South Dakota is known by which name?
questions.explain: More than 250 Lakota men, women and children were killed at Wounded Knee Creek in December 1890.

questions.q: What did the Homestead Act of 1862 offer settlers?
options: 160 acres of land if they farmed it for five years
Free train tickets to the West
A share of California gold claims
Cash to build a house in town
questions.explain: Over its long life the Homestead Act transferred about 270 million acres, roughly a tenth of all U.S. land, to settlers.

questions.q: The rallying cry 'Remember the Maine!' is linked to which war?
questions.explain: The battleship Maine exploded in Havana harbor in February 1898. War with Spain followed that April.

questions.q: Which future president led the 'Rough Riders' cavalry unit in Cuba in 1898?
questions.explain: Roosevelt became a national hero after the charge up the San Juan heights and was elected vice president in 1900.

questions.q: The teddy bear was named after which president?
questions.explain: After a 1902 hunting trip on which Roosevelt refused to shoot a captured bear, toy makers began selling 'Teddy's bears.'

questions.q: Which president summed up his foreign policy as 'Speak softly and carry a big stick'?
questions.explain: Roosevelt meant using diplomacy backed by military power, especially in Latin America.

questions.q: Theodore Roosevelt became president in 1901 after which president was assassinated?
questions.explain: McKinley was shot at the Pan-American Exposition in Buffalo, New York, and died eight days later.

questions.q: Which educator founded the Tuskegee Institute in Alabama in 1881?
questions.explain: Booker T. Washington built Tuskegee from a one-room school into a major college stressing practical training.

questions.q: Which Tuskegee scientist became famous for his work with peanuts and sweet potatoes?
questions.explain: George Washington Carver developed hundreds of products from peanuts and other crops to help Southern farmers.

questions.q: Which civil rights organization was founded in 1909 by W.E.B. Du Bois and others?
questions.explain: The National Association for the Advancement of Colored People fought segregation and lynching in the courts and the press.

questions.q: What were Jim Crow laws?
options: Southern laws that enforced racial segregation
Laws that set up public schools
questions.explain: Jim Crow laws segregated schools, trains and other public places across the South from the 1870s into the 1960s.

questions.q: Which Black journalist led a campaign against lynching in the 1890s?
questions.explain: Ida B. Wells began her anti-lynching reporting in Memphis in 1892 and later helped found the NAACP.

questions.q: The 1911 Triangle Shirtwaist Factory fire, which killed 146 garment workers, happened in which city?
questions.explain: Locked doors trapped many workers, mostly young immigrant women. The fire led to new safety laws in New York.

questions.q: Which amendment, ratified in 1913, allowed Congress to collect a federal income tax?
questions.explain: Before the 16th Amendment, the federal government relied mostly on tariffs and excise taxes.

questions.q: After the 17th Amendment of 1913, how are U.S. senators chosen?
options: Directly by the voters of each state
questions.explain: Before 1913, state legislatures chose senators. The change was a major Progressive Era reform.

questions.q: The 'unsinkable' Titanic sank in April 1912 after hitting what?
questions.explain: More than 1,500 people died when the Titanic sank in the North Atlantic on its first voyage.

questions.q: Which leader of the women's suffrage movement was arrested for voting in the 1872 election?
questions.explain: Susan B. Anthony was fined $100 for voting in Rochester, New York, and refused to pay.

questions.q: The 1848 meeting in New York that launched the organized women's rights movement is known as what?
questions.explain: At Seneca Falls, Elizabeth Cady Stanton read a Declaration of Sentiments modeled on the Declaration of Independence.

questions.q: What did the 19th Amendment, ratified in 1920, guarantee to women?
options: The right to serve in the army
The right to sit on juries
questions.explain: The 19th Amendment barred denying the vote on account of sex, ending a struggle of more than 70 years.

questions.q: In 1917, suffragists known as the 'Silent Sentinels' held signs outside which building?
questions.explain: Alice Paul's National Woman's Party picketed the White House to press President Wilson; many were arrested and jailed.

questions.q: Who became the first woman elected to Congress, in 1916?
questions.explain: Jeannette Rankin of Montana won a House seat four years before the 19th Amendment. She voted against entering both world wars.

questions.q: Who became the first woman to serve in a president's cabinet, as Franklin Roosevelt's Secretary of Labor?
questions.explain: Frances Perkins served from 1933 to 1945 and helped design Social Security and the minimum wage.

questions.q: In which year did the United States enter World War I?
questions.explain: The war began in Europe in 1914. Congress declared war on Germany in April 1917.

questions.q: Who was president when the United States fought in World War I?
questions.explain: Woodrow Wilson won reelection in 1916 partly on keeping the country out of war, then asked Congress to declare war in 1917.

questions.q: Which international organization did Woodrow Wilson propose after World War I, though the U.S. Senate refused to join it?
questions.explain: The Senate rejected the Treaty of Versailles, so the United States never joined the League of Nations.

questions.q: The 1915 sinking of which British passenger ship by a German submarine killed 128 Americans?
questions.explain: The Lusitania sinking turned many Americans against Germany two years before the U.S. entered the war.

questions.q: November 11, the day fighting in World War I ended in 1918, is now celebrated as which holiday?
questions.explain: It began as Armistice Day and was renamed Veterans Day in 1954 to honor veterans of all wars.

questions.q: The Tomb of the Unknown Soldier at Arlington was created in 1921 to honor an unidentified soldier from which war?
questions.explain: An unknown American killed in France was buried at Arlington on November 11, 1921. Unknowns from later wars were added.

questions.q: American soldiers in World War I were often given which nickname?
questions.explain: The nickname's origin is uncertain, but 'doughboys' was the common name for American infantrymen in World War I.

questions.q: The deadly flu pandemic that swept the world in 1918, near the end of World War I, is commonly called what?
questions.explain: The 1918 flu killed an estimated 50 million people worldwide, including about 675,000 Americans.

questions.q: Which general commanded the American forces sent to Europe in World War I?
questions.explain: General John 'Black Jack' Pershing led the American Expeditionary Forces and is buried at Arlington.

questions.q: The famous 'I Want YOU' recruiting poster of Uncle Sam was first made during which war?
questions.explain: James Montgomery Flagg drew the poster in 1917. About four million copies were printed during World War I.

questions.q: Louis Armstrong and Duke Ellington were stars of which music style that boomed in the 1920s?
questions.explain: Jazz grew from Black musical traditions in New Orleans and spread north. The 1920s are often called the Jazz Age.

questions.q: Young women of the 1920s who wore short skirts and bobbed hair were nicknamed what?
questions.explain: Flappers challenged old ideas about how women should dress and act, and became a symbol of the Roaring Twenties.

questions.q: The Harlem Renaissance, a flowering of Black art, music and writing in the 1920s, was centered in which city?
questions.explain: Harlem, a neighborhood in upper Manhattan, drew Black writers, artists and musicians during the Great Migration.

questions.q: Which poet was a leading figure of the Harlem Renaissance?
questions.explain: Langston Hughes wrote poems such as 'The Negro Speaks of Rivers' and 'I, Too,' celebrating Black life.

questions.q: Who made the first nonstop solo flight across the Atlantic Ocean, in 1927?
questions.explain: Lindbergh flew from New York to Paris in about 33 and a half hours in May 1927 and became a world celebrity.

questions.q: What was the name of Charles Lindbergh's plane, now in the National Air and Space Museum?
questions.explain: Lindbergh named the plane for the St. Louis businessmen who paid for it.

questions.q: Which pilot became the first woman to fly solo across the Atlantic, in 1932?
questions.explain: Amelia Earhart flew from Newfoundland to Northern Ireland. She disappeared over the Pacific in 1937.

questions.q: Which baseball star hit 60 home runs for the New York Yankees in 1927?
questions.explain: Babe Ruth's 60 home runs set a single-season record that stood until 1961.

questions.q: During Prohibition, secret illegal bars were often called what?
questions.explain: Customers had to 'speak easy,' or quietly, about these hidden bars, which often paid off police to stay open.

questions.q: Which Chicago gangster grew rich selling illegal alcohol during Prohibition?
questions.explain: Al Capone was finally convicted in 1931, not for bootlegging but for income tax evasion.

questions.q: Which amendment began Prohibition, the national ban on making and selling alcohol?
questions.explain: The 18th Amendment was ratified in 1919 and took effect in January 1920.

questions.q: Which amendment ended Prohibition in 1933?
questions.explain: The 21st Amendment repealed the 18th. It is the only amendment that cancels an earlier one.

questions.q: Released in 1927, which film is known as the first feature-length 'talkie' with spoken dialogue?
questions.explain: The Jazz Singer, starring Al Jolson, mixed silent scenes with songs and a few spoken lines, and began the end of the silent film era.

questions.q: The 1925 Scopes 'Monkey Trial' in Tennessee was about teaching what in public schools?
questions.explain: Teacher John Scopes was found guilty of teaching evolution in violation of state law, though the verdict was later overturned on a technicality.

questions.q: Which F. Scott Fitzgerald novel of 1925 portrays wealth and wild parties in the Roaring Twenties?
questions.explain: The Great Gatsby follows the mysterious millionaire Jay Gatsby on Long Island. The other titles are by Hemingway and Sinclair Lewis.

questions.q: Which 1920s president was nicknamed 'Silent Cal' for his quiet manner?
questions.explain: Calvin Coolidge became president when Harding died in 1923 and was known for saying very little.

questions.q: The Teapot Dome bribery scandal of the 1920s struck which president's administration?
questions.explain: Harding's interior secretary, Albert Fall, took bribes to lease government oil reserves and went to prison.

questions.q: Mount Rushmore, carved between 1927 and 1941, is in which state?
questions.explain: Mount Rushmore in the Black Hills shows Washington, Jefferson, Theodore Roosevelt and Lincoln.

questions.q: Completed in 1931, which New York skyscraper was the world's tallest building for nearly 40 years?
questions.explain: Built in just over a year, the Empire State Building held the title until the World Trade Center passed it around 1970.

questions.q: The stock market crash of October 29, 1929, which helped start the Great Depression, is often called what?
questions.explain: On Black Tuesday investors dumped millions of shares, and stock prices kept sliding for nearly three years.

questions.q: Who was president when the stock market crashed in 1929?
questions.explain: Herbert Hoover took office in March 1929, seven months before the crash, and lost the 1932 election to Roosevelt.

questions.q: During the Depression, shantytowns built by homeless people were mockingly named after which president?
questions.explain: People called them Hoovervilles, blaming the president for the hard times. A newspaper used as a blanket was a 'Hoover blanket.'

questions.q: The Dust Bowl of the 1930s struck farms mainly in which region?
questions.explain: Drought, heat and over-plowing turned parts of Oklahoma, Texas, Kansas, Colorado and New Mexico into blowing dust.

questions.q: Which John Steinbeck novel tells of an Oklahoma family fleeing the Dust Bowl for California?
options: The Old Man and the Sea
questions.explain: The Grapes of Wrath, published in 1939, follows the Joad family and won the Pulitzer Prize.

questions.q: What was the name of Franklin D. Roosevelt's set of programs to fight the Great Depression?
questions.explain: The Square Deal was Theodore Roosevelt's, the Fair Deal was Truman's and the Great Society was Lyndon Johnson's.

questions.q: Franklin D. Roosevelt spoke to Americans directly in radio talks known as what?
questions.explain: Roosevelt gave about 30 fireside chats from 1933 to 1944, explaining banking, the New Deal and the war in plain language.

questions.q: Which 1935 New Deal law created federal old-age pensions?
questions.explain: The Social Security Act also created unemployment insurance. The first monthly checks went out in 1940.

questions.q: How many times was Franklin D. Roosevelt elected president?
questions.explain: Roosevelt won in 1932, 1936, 1940 and 1944, the only president elected more than twice. He died early in his fourth term.

questions.q: Franklin D. Roosevelt lost the use of his legs after an illness in 1921. Which disease was he diagnosed with?
questions.explain: Roosevelt was diagnosed with polio at age 39. A statue at the FDR Memorial shows him in his wheelchair.

questions.q: In his 1933 inaugural address, Franklin Roosevelt said 'the only thing we have to fear is' what?
questions.explain: Roosevelt spoke at the depth of the Depression, with banks failing and about a quarter of workers unemployed.

questions.q: Which First Lady traveled the country as her husband's 'eyes and ears' during the Depression and World War II?
questions.explain: Eleanor Roosevelt wrote a daily newspaper column and later helped draft the Universal Declaration of Human Rights.

questions.q: Franklin Roosevelt's Scottish terrier, shown beside him in a statue at the FDR Memorial, was named what?
questions.explain: Fala traveled almost everywhere with Roosevelt. Checkers was Nixon's dog and Laddie Boy was Harding's.

questions.q: Hoover Dam, built in the 1930s on the Arizona-Nevada border, holds back which river?
questions.explain: Hoover Dam created Lake Mead and supplies water and power to much of the Southwest.

questions.q: In 1932, thousands of World War I veterans known as the Bonus Army camped in Washington to demand what?
questions.explain: Army troops drove the veterans out of their camps in July 1932, which badly hurt President Hoover's image.

questions.q: Until its own building opened in 1935, where did the Supreme Court usually meet?
questions.explain: The Court met in the Capitol from 1801 to 1935, apart from a few years after the 1814 fire, and used the Old Senate Chamber from 1860.

questions.q: In 1939, after being barred from Constitution Hall, which singer gave a famous concert on the steps of the Lincoln Memorial?
questions.explain: About 75,000 people heard Marian Anderson sing on Easter Sunday 1939, with Eleanor Roosevelt's support.

questions.q: Which American track star won four gold medals at the 1936 Olympics in Nazi Germany?
questions.explain: Jesse Owens's wins in Berlin undercut Hitler's claims of racial superiority.

questions.q: Pearl Harbor, the naval base attacked on December 7, 1941, is in which present-day state?
questions.explain: Hawaii was a U.S. territory in 1941 and became the 50th state in 1959.

questions.q: Which country's planes attacked Pearl Harbor in 1941?
questions.explain: The surprise attack sank or damaged 19 U.S. ships and killed about 2,400 Americans.

questions.q: Franklin Roosevelt called December 7, 1941, 'a date which will live in' what?
questions.explain: Roosevelt spoke to a joint session of Congress the next day, and Congress declared war on Japan within an hour.

questions.q: On D-Day, June 6, 1944, Allied troops landed on beaches in which region of France?
questions.explain: More than 150,000 Allied troops crossed the English Channel on D-Day to begin freeing Western Europe.

questions.q: Which American general was supreme commander of the Allied forces on D-Day?
questions.explain: Dwight Eisenhower planned and led the Normandy invasion and was elected president in 1952.

questions.q: In World War II, Germany, Italy and Japan were known by which name?
questions.explain: The Allies, including the United States, Britain and the Soviet Union, fought the Axis. The Central Powers fought in World War I.

questions.q: Who led Nazi Germany during World War II?
questions.explain: Adolf Hitler took power in 1933. Mussolini led Italy, Stalin the Soviet Union, and the Kaiser ruled Germany in World War I.

questions.q: What name is given to Nazi Germany's murder of about six million European Jews?
questions.explain: The Holocaust also killed millions of others, including Roma, disabled people and Soviet prisoners of war.

questions.q: Which wartime symbol, named in a 1942 song, stood for the millions of women who took factory jobs in World War II?
questions.explain: Rosie came from a 1942 song and a 1943 Norman Rockwell cover. The 'We Can Do It!' poster is now widely linked with her.

questions.q: What was the code name of the secret U.S. program that built the first atomic bombs?
questions.explain: The Manhattan Project employed about 130,000 people. Overlord was D-Day and Torch was the 1942 North Africa landing.

questions.q: The famous 1945 photo of Marines raising the flag, later the model for the Marine Corps War Memorial near Arlington, was taken on which island?
questions.explain: Joe Rosenthal took the photo on February 23, 1945. The bronze memorial was dedicated in 1954.

questions.q: During World War II, the U.S. government forced about 120,000 people of what ancestry into camps?
questions.explain: Most were American citizens. In 1988 Congress formally apologized and paid survivors $20,000 each.

questions.q: The Tuskegee Airmen of World War II were famous as the first group of what?
questions.explain: The Tuskegee Airmen trained in Alabama and flew fighter escort missions over Europe with a strong record.

questions.q: Marine 'code talkers' in the Pacific sent unbreakable messages in the language of which Native American people?
questions.explain: About 400 Navajo code talkers served. The Japanese never broke their code.

questions.q: What did V-E Day in May 1945 celebrate?
options: Japan's surrender, ending the war in Asia
The landing of Allied troops in France
Germany's surrender, ending the war in Europe
The end of the fighting in World War I
questions.explain: Germany surrendered on May 7-8, 1945. Japan surrendered in August, and the formal signing was on September 2.

questions.q: Who was Britain's prime minister for most of World War II?
questions.explain: Winston Churchill took office in May 1940 and led Britain until July 1945.

questions.q: Which June 1942 naval battle is considered the turning point of the war in the Pacific?
questions.explain: At Midway, U.S. planes sank four Japanese aircraft carriers, and Japan never regained the upper hand at sea.

questions.q: The GI Bill of 1944 helped returning World War II veterans pay for what?
questions.explain: Millions of veterans went to college or bought homes with GI Bill help, which fueled postwar growth.

questions.q: In which year did World War II end?
questions.explain: Germany surrendered in May 1945 and Japan in August 1945, after the atomic bombings.

questions.q: Which battleship, sunk at Pearl Harbor with more than 1,100 of its crew, now has a memorial built over it?
questions.explain: The USS Arizona Memorial opened in 1962. Japan signed its surrender aboard the USS Missouri in 1945.

questions.q: The Pentagon, headquarters of the Department of Defense, was built during which war?
questions.explain: Construction began on September 11, 1941, and the building was finished in January 1943, in about 16 months.

questions.q: Which president, who led the nation in World War I, is buried in Washington National Cathedral?
questions.explain: Woodrow Wilson stayed in Washington after leaving office and was buried at the cathedral in 1924. Taft is at Arlington.

questions.q: During the Great Migration, millions of Black Americans moved from the rural South to where?
options: Cities in the North and West
questions.explain: About six million Black Southerners moved between about 1910 and 1970, escaping Jim Crow and seeking jobs.

questions.q: Which country, at war with Germany since 1939, became the main European ally of the United States in World War II?
questions.explain: Britain declared war on Germany in 1939. Spain, Sweden and Switzerland stayed neutral.

questions.q: The first atomic bomb used in war was dropped in August 1945 on Japan. Which president decided to use it?
questions.explain: Truman approved the bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki. Japan announced its surrender days later.

questions.q: Which leader of the Soviet Union met with Roosevelt and Churchill at Yalta in 1945?
questions.explain: At the Yalta Conference in February 1945 the 'Big Three' planned for the defeat of Germany and the postwar world.

questions.q: Which general led U.S. forces in the Pacific and famously promised the Philippines 'I shall return'?
questions.explain: Douglas MacArthur left the Philippines in 1942 and returned in October 1944. He accepted Japan's surrender in 1945.

questions.q: Which country was led by Benito Mussolini during World War II?
questions.explain: Mussolini ruled Italy from 1922. He was overthrown in 1943 and killed by Italian partisans in 1945.

questions.q: The war in Europe began in September 1939 when Germany invaded which country?
questions.explain: Britain and France declared war on Germany two days after the invasion of Poland.

questions.q: During World War II, the government issued ration books to limit how much Americans could buy of which items?
questions.explain: Rationing kept scarce goods flowing to the military. Coffee, butter and tires were also rationed.

questions.q: In the late 1800s, which form of transportation linked the country together and helped cities like Chicago boom?
questions.explain: By 1900 the country had about 190,000 miles of railroad track, more than all of Europe.

questions.q: Which new entertainment brought news, music and comedy into most American homes in the 1920s and 1930s?
questions.explain: Commercial radio began in 1920. By the late 1930s most American households owned a radio.

questions.q: What famous New York statue welcomed many immigrants as their ships arrived after 1886?
questions.explain: Lady Liberty stands on Liberty Island, near Ellis Island, in New York Harbor.

questions.q: What was the name of the group of 11 Southern states that left the Union in 1860-1861?
questions.explain: The Confederacy wrote its own constitution and chose Jefferson Davis as president.

questions.q: Which word was used for the countries, including the United States, Britain and the Soviet Union, that fought against Germany in World War II?
questions.explain: The Allies were led by the 'Big Three': Roosevelt, Churchill and Stalin.

questions.q: What did Henry Ford's moving assembly line, introduced in 1913, mainly make possible?
options: Cars that could run on electricity
Building cars faster and more cheaply
questions.explain: The assembly line cut the time to build a Model T from about 12 hours to about 90 minutes.
